text: Merging stones, palindromes, painting.
stones 2 5 3 1 fill by length: diagonal 1, 2, 3, 4 answer f[1][4] = 22

Interval DP (区间动态规划): the state is a segment, f[l][r] = the best answer for a[l..r]. A segment is built from two shorter segments, so compute by increasing length. Merging stones in a line (P1775): f[l][r] = min over split k of f[l][k] + f[k+1][r] + (sum of a[l..r]).
The last merge joins a[l..k] and a[k+1..r]; whatever happened before, that merge costs the whole sum, which a prefix sum gives in O(1). n² states × n splits = O(n³).
Loop order: length outside, left end inside. Looping l from 1 to n and r upward would read f[k+1][r] before it is ready. A safe alternative is l from n down to 1 and r from l up.
f[l][l] = 0 (a single pile costs nothing), and only segments of length ≥ 2 take the minimum. Initialise those to a large value, not 0, or the min stays 0.

Palindromes are naturally interval problems: look at the two ends. If they match, they pair up and the inside remains. If not, one end must be matched by an inserted character (P1435).
Equivalently: answer = n − (longest palindromic subsequence) = n − LCS(s, reverse s). For length 2, f[l+1] [r−1] is an empty segment (l+1 > r−1), whose value 0 is already in the array.
AAAAA
RGBGR

Painting a strip (P4170 涂色): each stroke paints a segment one colour; later strokes cover earlier ones. If both ends have the same colour, the first stroke can be stretched to cover both, so the end costs nothing extra. Otherwise the strip splits into two independent parts.
RGBGR: one R stroke over everything, then G over the middle three, then B in the centre: 3. Interval DPs often combine "the ends are special" with "split somewhere".
Doubling the array; min and max; the energy necklace.
a ring of n becomes a line of 2n; each window of length n is one place to cut
Ring DP (环形动态规划): piles on a circle can also merge pile n with pile 1.

Break the circle by copying the array after itself: a[n+i] = a[i]. Every way to merge the circle never merges across one gap, so it is a line of n consecutive piles, a window [i, i + n − 1] of the doubled array.
Run the line DP on the doubled array of length 2n (segments up to length n only), then answer = best f[i][i + n − 1] over i = 1 … n. Still O(n³), with a factor of about 8.
Stones on a circle, both the minimum and the maximum total cost (P1880). The sum of the segment is added once after the split loop, since it does not depend on k.
The maximum is not "the minimum turned around": each needs its own table. For n = 4 piles 4 5 9 4 the best cut gives 43 and the worst gives 54.

Energy necklace (P1063): each bead is (head, tail) and neighbours share a value, like matrix-chain multiplication on a ring. Merging two blocks releases head × middle × tail. The tail of bead r is e[r + 1], so the doubled array needs index 2n as well.
Polygon (P4342) adds negative numbers and × edges: a maximum can come from two minima multiplied (−3 × −4), so keep both min and max for every segment and combine all four products.

Other shapes of interval DP: 关路灯(P1220) walks out from a starting point, state [l, r] plus "standing at the left or right end"; 合唱队(P3205) builds a queue by adding to either end, again "which end was last"; Zuma (CF607B) removes palindromes with f[l][r] and the ends-match rule.
